title: Canada Pension Plan
subtitle: Decode what decades of contributions may become each month

blocks.text: CPP does not reward the person who remembers every pay stub since 1984. It does like a clean contribution record, so the old filing cabinet may finally get a supporting role.

The Canada Pension Plan retirement pension is a taxable monthly payment. It is based mainly on the CPP you paid in, your earnings and the age you start. You usually need to be at least 60 and have made at least one valid payment into CPP. Workers in Quebec normally pay into the Quebec Pension Plan instead.
In 2026, the most a new CPP retirement pension pays at age 65 is $1,507.65 a month. The April 2026 average for people just starting was $877.01. Most people do not get the top amount.

items.title: “Everyone receives the advertised maximum CPP at 65.”
items.text: The top amount assumes you paid in strongly for many years. Your own record and start age set your amount. The headline top amount is not a retirement participation trophy.

blocks.text: Service Canada: CPP retirement pension
Knowing what sets your own CPP amount lets you plan on your real number, not the headline.
blocks.detail: Your contribution record, a few protections and the age you start decide what you will get each month.
blocks.extra: Section 02 breaks your estimate into four parts.

items.title: CONTRIBUTION HISTORY
items.text: Your Statement of Contributions lists your earnings and what you paid into CPP. Look into missing or wrong years before you treat an estimate as final.

items.title: EARNINGS PATTERN
items.text: CPP looks at how much and how long you paid in. The base part can leave out some low-earning years. The newer enhanced part has its own rules.

items.title: PROTECTIONS
items.text: Rules for raising children, disability and low earnings can protect your amount when you meet their conditions.

items.title: START AGE
items.text: Your pension goes up or down for good depending on the month it starts, before or after age 65.

blocks.text: The base CPP math may leave out up to eight of your lowest-earning years. The enhanced part usually uses your best 40 years. Service Canada applies the exact rules.
If you were the main caregiver of a child under seven and meet the rules, the child-rearing provision may leave low or zero-earning months out of the base math, or add credits to the enhanced part.

items.title: “A zero-earning year always lowers CPP by the same amount.”
items.text: Rules for low earnings, raising children and disability can change how low-earning years count. The calendar contains years. The formula contains exceptions.

blocks.text: Service Canada: CPP amount

sections.title: Early, Standard or Late Is a Choice, Not a Ranking

blocks.text: Starting before 65 lowers CPP by 0.6% for each month early, up to a 36% cut at 60. Waiting past 65 raises it by 0.7% a month, up to a 42% boost at 70. Waiting past 70 adds nothing more.
The change for your start age is permanent. Compare your household cash, health, work plans, taxes, savings and what a surviving partner would need, not only a break-even age.
CPP does not start on its own. Apply ahead of time through My Service Canada Account or by paper. When you decide, think about your other taxable income and income-based benefits like GIS.
CPP is taxable. Tax is not taken off unless you ask, so plan for it before the first deposit starts looking entirely spendable.

items.title: “Starting CPP at 60 is always a mistake, or always the smart move.”
items.text: No age wins for everyone. How long you expect to live, how much cash you need, work, savings, taxes and other benefits can point to different good choices.

blocks.text: Key takeaway
Check your contribution record, claim every protection that applies, then compare start dates as part of your whole retirement income plan.

sections.title: Retirement Can Still Have a Paycheque

blocks.text: You can work while you get CPP. From 60 to 65, a working recipient usually keeps paying into CPP. From 65 to 70, an employee can choose to stop with CRA Form CPT30. If not, payments into CPP continue. They end at 70.

Those payments build a separate Post-Retirement Benefit, or PRB, paid for life. It is usually added on its own the next year. Each year of work that qualifies can add another PRB. In 2026, the most a new PRB pays at 65 is $54.69 a month. Your real amount depends on your earnings, payments and age.

Sharing a pension with a current spouse is different from splitting credits for good after a separation or divorce. Both differ from CRA pension income splitting. Similar words, separate forms, no group project.

sections.title: Priya and the Maximum That Wasn’t Hers

blocks.text: Meet Priya
paragraphs: Priya Nair lives in Mississauga and wants to stop working at 61 to help with her new grandson. She finds the 2026 top CPP amount online and puts it straight into her budget. The number looks official, confident and dressed for the occasion.

Then she logs in to My Service Canada Account. Her own estimate is much lower. Priya moved to Canada at 38, and she spent several years caring for her kids on little or no pay. The top amount assumed a work history she never had.
Her friend says to apply at 60 anyway and stop worrying, since “it’s all the same in the end.” Priya is tempted. She is tired, and the baby is due in the spring.

Before she signs anything, she decides to check her record line by line. She finds one year with no earnings at all, even though she worked full time that year. She sends Service Canada her old T4 slip. She also asks about the years she stayed home with her children.
The twist is good news. The fixed year and the child-rearing rule both raise her estimate. It is still below the top amount, and it is more than she feared.

Priya compares starting at 61, 65 and 70, using her real estimate, her taxes and her savings. She picks 63. That gives her two years with her grandson on her savings, and a bigger CPP for the rest of her life.
Her plan is smaller on paper and stronger in real life. The headline number gets permission to retire from her budget.

blocks.text: The best CPP comparison uses the same checked record at several start ages. Do not compare your age-60 estimate with someone else’s age-70 top amount.
Priya raised her CPP estimate by fixing one missing year and claiming her years at home with her kids.
blocks.detail: Checking your own Statement of Contributions can turn a guess into a number you can plan around.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 06 tests whether you can choose the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: What two basic conditions make you eligible for a CPP retirement pension?
items.detail: You usually must be at least 60 and have made at least one valid payment into CPP.

items.title: Why do most people get less than the top amount?
items.detail: The top amount assumes you paid in strongly for many years. Your own record and start age set your amount.

items.title: How does starting at 60 change the age-65 amount?
items.detail: It lowers CPP by 0.6% for each month early, which adds up to the largest cut, 36%, at age 60.

items.title: What can the child-rearing rule protect?
items.detail: It may leave low or zero-earning months out of the base math, or add credits to the enhanced part.

items.title: Why think about taxes and GIS before you pick a start date?
items.detail: CPP counts as taxable income. It can change your household cash and income-based benefits like GIS.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): CPP Start-Date Decision File

blocks.text: Use rounded numbers and short labels. Check your own estimates and records through official Service Canada channels.
A missing earnings year can follow you for decades. Review your Statement of Contributions early, so you have time to find T4 slips, tax notices or employer records.

items.title: CPP
items.text: Canada Pension Plan retirement pension. It is taxable.

items.title: Statement of Contributions
items.text: Service Canada’s record of your CPP earnings and payments.

items.title: General drop-out
items.text: Leaving some low-earning years out of part of the math.

items.title: Child-rearing provision
items.text: Protection for years you cared for a child under seven.

items.title: PRB
items.text: Post-Retirement Benefit. Extra pension you build by paying into CPP after it starts.

items.title: Credit split
items.text: Dividing CPP credits for good after a relationship ends.

items.title: CPT30
items.text: The CRA form workers aged 65 to 69 can use to stop paying into CPP.
